questions.question_text: The systems approach to family therapy

options.text: places more emphasis on the meaning of a child’s symptoms for the larger family than on the child’s specific symptoms
maintains that all things are interdependent and nothing changes without everything else changing
sees symptoms as serving a purpose for the family system
views each family member as acting in a way that opposes symptomatic improvement in the presenting patient

questions.explanation: The systems approach, a departure from so-called “linear theories,” uses cybernetics and general systems theory[cite: 14]. Whereas cybernetics holds that systems maintain an equilibrium, general systems theory describes all living systems as existing in tension between homeostasis and change[cite: 14]. All components of a family are interdependent, and nothing changes without everything else changing accordingly[cite: 14]. In this approach to family problems, symptoms are seen not as residing within the child but rather as serving a purpose for the entire family system[cite: 14]. These symptoms provide systemic survival and maintain homeostasis[cite: 14]. Each family member is presumed to act in a way that opposes symptomatic improvement in the presenting patient[cite: 14]. Family-systems theorists attempt to counteract this hypothetical process in treatment; they believe that one must destabilize the family system to promote change[cite: 14]. The formulation for a family-systems therapist emphasizes the meaning that symptoms have for the family[cite: 14]. Problem-maintaining patterns are observed, and these patterns are interrupted[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: With regard to adverse effects of medications in children and adolescents,

options.text: tardive dyskinesia has not been observed in this age group
withdrawal dyskinesias do occur in this age group
anticholinergic and cardiovascular side effects are rarely seen in this age group
there is less risk for adverse effects in this age group compared with adults

correct_answer.text: withdrawal dyskinesias do occur in this age group

correct_answers.text: withdrawal dyskinesias do occur in this age group

questions.explanation:
Even though they may metabolize medications more rapidly than adults, children are at no less risk than adults for adverse effects of medications and in some cases are at increased risk[cite: 14]. Clinicians must therefore know the adverse-effect profiles of all medications being prescribed, as well as how to manage adverse effects should they arise[cite: 14].
Many of the adverse effects of antipsychotic, antidepressant, and mood-stabilizing medications seen in adults are also seen in children and adolescents[cite: 14]. Of particular concern are the anticholinergic and cardiovascular effects of the tricyclic medications and the extrapyramidal effects of the antipsychotics[cite: 14]. Withdrawal dyskinesias are more common than tardive dyskinesia among children and adolescents, although both have been observed in this age group[cite: 14].
The best policy is usually to start with low dosage and titrate slowly upward to therapeutic effect[cite: 14]. Use of the lowest possible maintenance doses in the therapeutic range can minimize adverse effects[cite: 14]. Monotherapy is preferable[cite: 14]. Targeted combined pharmacotherapy may be necessary in children with multiple disorders but should be used with caution to minimize adverse effects[cite: 14]. Table 53.1 lists common adverse effects of medications[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: Which theorist described a series of “developmental pathways,” for example, a pathway that connects a child’s capacity to play to the adult’s capacity to work?
questions.explanation:
Child psychotherapy began with Sigmund Freud’s case of Little Hans, a 5-year old boy with phobia[cite: 14]. Published in 1909, the case was the first description of the psychotherapeutic treatment of a child[cite: 14]. The therapy in the case was actually rendered by Hans’s father, who reported to Freud and received guidance from him[cite: 14]. Significant interest in the mental and emotional lives of children was generated by Freud’s theory of psychosexual development, which posited that symptoms in adulthood could be traced to conflicts arising at earlier stages of development[cite: 14].
Decades later, Anna Freud and Melanie Klein developed the field of child psychoanalysis[cite: 14]. Klein understood play to be the childhood equivalent of free association in adults[cite: 14]. She explored early object relations; the role of primitive defenses such as projection, projective identification, and omnipotent control; the process of early identifications; and the role of envy and guilt in these early relationships[cite: 14]. Anna Freud looked at play from a psychoanalytic perspective and learned about the child from the play but did not view play as a substitute for free association[cite: 14]. Her work concerned the development of the ego, the evolution of defenses, and the developmental pathway of various ego functions[cite: 14]. In one example of a developmental pathway, she described a continuity from the child’s capacity to play to the adult’s capacity to work[cite: 14].
There were several other major early contributors to the field[cite: 14]. Donald Winnicott emphasized the importance of the mother–infant relationship[cite: 14]. His understanding of the transitional object, for instance, as playing a role in the child’s ability to separate from the maternal figure instilled a new appreciation of the meaning of commonly observed childhood behaviors[cite: 14]. Margaret Mahler observed mother–toddler interactions in a systemized way and described the evolution of early object relations from the perspective of separation and individuation[cite: 14]. August Aichorn first extended psychoanalytic work to delinquent adolescents[cite: 14]. Jean Piaget focused on children’s cognitive development[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is useful in the treatment of which of the following disorders or situations?

options.text: Adolescent depression in a group setting

questions.explanation:
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the most extensively, thoroughly researched therapy in use today for the treatment of psychological problems in children and adolescents[cite: 14]. CBT can be used in both individual and group settings[cite: 14].
Children with conduct disorder may be impulsive, oppositional, defiant, moody, and angry[cite: 14]. During assessment, the therapist gauges the child’s thought processes in addressing a variety of situations[cite: 14]. The child is then taught a step-by-step approach to solving problems[cite: 14]. In this training, the child is guided to develop skills in appraising situations and making appropriate decisions for action[cite: 14]. This technique may be adapted to accommodate children ages 4 years through young adulthood[cite: 14]. The treatment uses structured tasks such as games, academic activities, and other age-appropriate tools[cite: 14]. The therapist plays an active role in the treatment, encouraging modeling via practice and role playing[cite: 14]. Punishment or withdrawal of privileges is used when necessary[cite: 14].
Individual CBT has been demonstrated to be an effective treatment for depression in adolescents[cite: 14]. Additionally, Peter Lewinsohn and colleagues developed the “Adolescents Coping with Depression Course,” which consists of 16 2-hour sessions conducted over an 8-week period for groups of up to 10 adolescents[cite: 14]. The program includes a psychoeducational component that aims to destigmatize depression, emphasize skills training to promote control over one’s mood, and enhance adolescents’ abilities to cope with problematic situations[cite: 14]. The group activities include role playing[cite: 14]. Social skills training occurs throughout the treatment to facilitate and enhance communication and includes teaching conversational techniques, planning social activities, and developing strategies for making friends[cite: 14]. Sessions are designed to increase participation in pleasant activities based on the assumption that depressed adolescents have few positively reinforcing activities in their lives[cite: 14]. Relaxation training is provided to enhance comfort in social settings and to offset anxiety[cite: 14]. Focus on changing depressogenic cognitions is provided by identifying, challenging, and changing negative thoughts and irrational beliefs[cite: 14]. The teens are also taught negotiating and problem-solving techniques[cite: 14].
John March and colleagues developed the CBT treatment, “How I Ran OCD Off My Land,” a manualized treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) in children and adolescents[cite: 14]. The treatment uses a variety of methods including exposure, response prevention, extinction, anxiety-management training, reinforcement, modeling and shaping, and habit reversal[cite: 14]. After the initial assessment, the child and family are first educated about OCD, placing the disorder in a neurobiological framework that identifies OCD as a medical condition[cite: 14]. Thereafter, the child learns to make OCD the “enemy” and is taught to “boss back” the OCD in order to gain a sense of agency in managing the anxiety that characterizes the disorder[cite: 14]. The parameters of symptoms are “mapped” to fully identify obsessions, compulsions, triggers, and avoidance behaviors[cite: 14]. The majority of subsequent sessions deal with anxiety-management techniques (e.g., relaxation, diaphragmatic breathing, and constructive self-talk) and exposure with response-prevention[cite: 14]. Exposure involves therapist-assisted imaginal and in vivo exposure, and response prevention consists of exercises in session coupled with weekly homework assignments[cite: 14]. Parents are trained to ally with the child to “boss back” OCD[cite: 14].
With regard to socially rejected children, Fred Frankel and colleagues developed the 12-session CBT called “Parent Assisted Social Skills Training.”[cite: 14] First, the child’s social network is examined, taking into account the family, home, school, and neighborhood to develop an integrated approach to treatment[cite: 14]. Children are seen in groups where they learn rules of peer etiquette[cite: 14]. They are also offered training skills to expand their peer networks, and parents and children are taught how to work together to promote more successful play dates and how to improve the child’s competence with non-aggressive responses to teasing and conflict with other children and adults[cite: 14]. Coached play is incorporated, and makes use of positive reinforcement and time outs as feedback for behaviors[cite: 14]. Child socialization homework is assigned, and didactic presentations are made to parents to inform them of their part in helping their children to gain peer acceptance, ensure that the parents adhere to assigned roles in the children’s homework assignments, and provide supportive feedback for the principles being taught[cite: 14]. Table 53.2 lists some of the techniques of CBT[cite: 14].

options.text: treatment with stimulant medication alone is maximally effective in older children and adolescents
stimulant medication equally improves the full range of symptoms of children with the disorder, including comorbid behavioral disturbances
treatment with stimulant medication alone tends to significantly improve outcomes for children with oppositional and aggressive behavior, academic underachievement, and poor peer relationships
the presence of aggression in children and parents is a strong predictor of poor outcome in treatment of ADHD

correct_answer.text: the presence of aggression in children and parents is a strong predictor of poor outcome in treatment of ADHD

correct_answers.text: the presence of aggression in children and parents is a strong predictor of poor outcome in treatment of ADHD

questions.explanation:
The best treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and its associated behavioral, academic, and social disruptions combines stimulant medication with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)[cite: 14]. Treatment with stimulant medication alone is effective but may not be maximally effective for ADHD, particularly in older children and adolescents[cite: 14]. Many children experience a reduction in symptoms, but impairment persists at clinically significant levels[cite: 14]. Although many children improve substantially with pharmacotherapy, many do not achieve full remission of symptoms even with adequate doses and trials of medication[cite: 14]. More children achieve remission with combination therapy[cite: 14].
Stimulant medication may not equally affect the full range of symptoms of children with ADHD and associated behavioral disturbances[cite: 14]. Although the primary symptoms of ADHD (inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity) may be greatly improved with medication, other primary or comorbid characteristics of the syndrome (e.g., oppositional and aggressive behavior, academic underachievement, and poor peer relationships) often do not respond to medication alone[cite: 14]. Because these associated features, together with family function, robustly predict long-term outcome of children with ADHD, treatment with stimulants alone may not significantly improve outcomes for these children[cite: 14]. These features are most effectively addressed with psychosocial interventions, particularly CBT[cite: 14]. Additionally, psychosocial treatments are sometimes the only therapies available to patients who do not respond to medications for primary symptoms of ADHD, who cannot tolerate medications because of side effects, or whose parents oppose the use of medications[cite: 14].
An additional limitation of stimulant treatment involves the complicating issue of home environment and home behavioral issues[cite: 14]. Stimulants cover 6 to 12 hours of the day, typically the times when children are in school or other organized activities outside the home[cite: 14]. This leaves parents on their own to manage impulsive, oppositional, and disruptive behaviors in the afternoons, evenings, weekends, and vacations[cite: 14]. When no other treatment is made available to them, parents may develop coercive, hostile, and overly punitive approaches to dealing with their children’s behaviors, which may in turn exacerbate the behavioral issues[cite: 14]. Child and parent aggression are among the best predictors of poor outcome in children with ADHD[cite: 14]. For all of these reasons, CBT continues to be used and evaluated both alone and in combination with medications in the treatment of children with ADHD[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: Parent–child conflict is a risk factor for

options.text: cognitive distortions that negatively bias perceptions

questions.explanation:
Parent–child conflict is a risk factor for depression, poor treatment outcome in depression, relapse after treatment for depression, and cognitive distortions that negatively bias perceptions[cite: 14]. As a result, including a parent–child relational component in treatment for depression is well justified[cite: 14]. Preliminary evidence suggests that addressing the parent–child relationship in treatment is more effective than treating the child alone[cite: 14]. Parents can be taught contingency management procedures along with alternative effective methods for parenting and creating a positive family environment[cite: 14]. Additionally, family interactions are targeted to shape and reinforce effective communication and to increase pleasant activities and positive affect in the home[cite: 14].
This parent–child treatment can be incorporated into cognitive behavioral treatment (CBT) of children and adolescents with depression, the psychotherapy modality most supported in the literature for treatment of this those with disorder[cite: 14]. CBT for depression is a skill-based treatment centered around the assumption that depression is caused and maintained by inadequate cognitive skills for coping with stress[cite: 14]. CBT posits that changes in behavior and cognition will lead to changes in emotions[cite: 14]. Among the behavioral and cognitive skills deficits that may characterize depressed youths are low involvement in pleasant activities, poor problem-solving and assertion skills, cognitive distortions that negatively bias perceptions, negative automatic thoughts, negative views of self and future, and failure to attribute positive outcomes to internal causes[cite: 14]. The therapist works with children or adolescents to help them reverse these patterns of thought and behavior[cite: 14]. Treatment is designed to improve the patients’ problem-solving ability when faced with stressful situations, including conflicts in their relationships with family members, particularly parents[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: In terms of pharmacokinetics, compared with adults, children have
questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetics in children differ from those in adults because children have greater (not lower) hepatic capacity, greater (not lower) glomerular filtration rates (GFR), less (not more) fatty tissue, and decreased (not increased) half-lives of many medications[cite: 14]. As a result of differences in hepatic capacity, GFR, and fatty tissue content, children tend to eliminate medications more rapidly than adults and to store less drug in fat[cite: 14]. Meanwhile, for many medications, there is little evidence that blood level corresponds in any predictable way to drug effect[cite: 14]. As a result, medications have to be dosed carefully in children, and dosing patterns and predicted responses in adults often do not apply to children and adolescents[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: A 12-year-old boy performs 3 hours of daily compulsive hand washing and has extreme difficulty going to school because of contamination fears.

options.text: Interpersonal, cognitive, or psychodynamic therapy plus fluoxetine
Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray plus behavioral conditioning
Inpatient unit with psychodynamic, family, and behavioral interventions

questions.explanation:
The majority of children who present for psychiatric treatment are brought in by family members who are concerned about the child’s functioning or who have followed up on suggestions from teachers or pediatricians[cite: 14]. Often, children do not express a desire for treatment, nor do they understand the degree to which they have caused concern in others[cite: 14]. Occasionally, an adolescent will ask a parent for help, but more often, distress in this age group is manifested by troubling behaviors[cite: 14]. To synthesize a useful treatment approach, it is generally necessary to understand the views of both the child and the parents[cite: 14]. In most cases, treatment consists of multiple modalities through which to manipulate the child’s environment positively as well as to influence the feelings and behaviors of the child[cite: 14]. The brief vignettes that follow exemplify the combined approach to addressing children’s and adolescents’ psychiatric needs[cite: 14].
A 12-year-old boy who presents with impairment caused by compulsive hand washing and obsessions regarding fears of contamination is a candidate for combined treatment with medication and behavioral therapy[cite: 14]. Several drugs from the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) class of medications, including sertraline (Zoloft), have established efficacy in reducing obsessions and compulsions in children and adolescents with obsessive-compulsive disorder[cite: 14]. The benefit of medication is enhanced when combined with response prevention, a form of behavioral therapy that diminishes compulsive behaviors by challenging the patient to tolerate the feared situation (e.g., fear that his hands are dirty) without carrying out the compulsion (e.g., washing)[cite: 14]. In this way, the child learns that the exposure to the situation will not have the feared negative effects, and anxiety thereby diminishes[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: A 10-year-old girl became oppositional and defiant shortly after her mother married a man with three children.

options.text: Interpersonal, cognitive, or psychodynamic therapy plus fluoxetine
Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray plus behavioral conditioning
Inpatient unit with psychodynamic, family, and behavioral interventions

questions.explanation: A 10-year-old girl who responds to a new family constellation with oppositional and defiant behaviors is expressing her discomfort about a major change in the family’s functioning[cite: 14]. Family therapy is a useful modality to understand the triggers, responses, and meanings of these behaviors to the family and to the child[cite: 14]. It is likely that when the child is given a forum in which to express her discomfort, the behaviors will diminish[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: A 15-year-old girl has lost 25 percent of her body weight and cannot control her purging behaviors.

options.text: Interpersonal, cognitive, or psychodynamic therapy plus fluoxetine
Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray plus behavioral conditioning
Inpatient unit with psychodynamic, family, and behavioral interventions

correct_answer.text: Inpatient unit with psychodynamic, family, and behavioral interventions

correct_answers.text: Inpatient unit with psychodynamic, family, and behavioral interventions

questions.explanation: A 15-year-old girl who has lost 25 percent of her body weight and cannot control her purging behaviors generally requires an inpatient setting in which to initiate treatment, to establish refeeding, and to observe her continuously to prevent purging[cite: 14]. Given the complex effects of starvation, a malnourished adolescent is not a good candidate for outpatient treatment[cite: 14]. The treatment approaches for the restricting and purging type of anorexia nervosa are multimodal[cite: 14]. A behavioral component is necessary to systematically address nutritional needs and to prevent behaviors that further increase malnutrition[cite: 14]. A family approach is needed to probe the family’s role in the disorder[cite: 14]. A psychodynamic approach may be beneficial to work with the adolescent in identifying the meaning of the disorder and the psychological forces that drive the behaviors[cite: 14]. Medications are sometimes used to treat concurrent anxiety and depression and to ameliorate bingeing and purging[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: A 17-year-old girl has recently been discharged from an inpatient unit after a suicide attempt in the midst of a severe depression.

options.text: Interpersonal, cognitive, or psychodynamic therapy plus fluoxetine
Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray plus behavioral conditioning
Inpatient unit with psychodynamic, family, and behavioral interventions

correct_answer.text: Interpersonal, cognitive, or psychodynamic therapy plus fluoxetine

correct_answers.text: Interpersonal, cognitive, or psychodynamic therapy plus fluoxetine

questions.explanation: A 17-year-old girl who has been discharged from an inpatient unit presumably is stable, not posing an imminent danger to herself, and is ready to engage in outpatient treatment[cite: 14]. Evidence suggests that fluoxetine (Prozac) is effective in the treatment of major depression in adolescents[cite: 14]. Medications are most effective when combined with psychotherapy; particularly after the potentially jarring effects of a suicide attempt and hospitalizations, psychotherapy (interpersonal, cognitive behavioral, or psychodynamic) is certainly indicated in this case[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old girl has not been in school for several weeks because she has been bothered by derogatory auditory hallucinations; she is not suicidal or homicidal.

options.text: Interpersonal, cognitive, or psychodynamic therapy plus fluoxetine
Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray plus behavioral conditioning
Inpatient unit with psychodynamic, family, and behavioral interventions

questions.explanation: A 14-year-old girl who has recently stopped attending school because of an increase in auditory hallucinations is in crisis[cite: 14]. Because she is not suicidal, she may not need the containment of an inpatient unit, but she would be a good candidate for a partial hospitalization program in which she can receive daily monitoring of antipsychotic medication as well as daily support and therapy from staff[cite: 14]. A return to an appropriate school setting would be a primary goal of the treatment[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: An 8-year-old boy will not attend sleepover parties because of his bedwetting.

options.text: Interpersonal, cognitive, or psychodynamic therapy plus fluoxetine
Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray plus behavioral conditioning
Inpatient unit with psychodynamic, family, and behavioral interventions

correct_answer.text: Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray plus behavioral conditioning

correct_answers.text: Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray plus behavioral conditioning

questions.explanation: Enuresis (in this case, in an 8-year-old boy) is much more common in boys than girls and may cause psychological distress and social difficulties for children who continue to have this problem into the school-age years[cite: 14]. Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray is effective in some children with enuresis and may be useful in the short term[cite: 14]. The most effective treatment, however, is a behavioral approach using methods such as the bell-and-pad conditioning treatment[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: A 7-year-old boy is about to be suspended from school because of his inability to sit in his seat and stay on task as well as his provocative behavior toward his classmates.

options.text: Interpersonal, cognitive, or psychodynamic therapy plus fluoxetine
Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray plus behavioral conditioning
Inpatient unit with psychodynamic, family, and behavioral interventions

questions.explanation: A 7-year-old boy who cannot stay on task and who is hyperactive and socially provocative is exhibiting typical symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)[cite: 14]. The treatment for the core symptoms is a stimulant medication such as methylphenidate (Ritalin)[cite: 14]. Most children with ADHD also have social difficulties and may be rejected by their peers[cite: 14]. Thus, it is often beneficial to include social skills groups as an additional therapeutic intervention[cite: 14].

questions.question_text: A 9-year-old boy has chronic vocal and motor tics, as well as significant impulsivity and frequent aggressive behavior toward his peers at school and siblings; this patient’s tics were severely exacerbated during a prior trial of methylphenidate.

options.text: Interpersonal, cognitive, or psychodynamic therapy plus fluoxetine
Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal spray plus behavioral conditioning
Inpatient unit with psychodynamic, family, and behavioral interventions

questions.explanation: A 9-year-old boy with both motor and vocal tics lasting longer than 1 year meets criteria for Tourette’s disorder; this diagnosis is very commonly comorbid with ADHD, which likely also exists in this patient, as evidenced by his hyperactive, impulsive, and aggressive behavior[cite: 14]. Treatment of comorbid ADHD and Tourette’s disorder is complicated by the fact that stimulant treatment can exacerbate tics in these patients[cite: 14]. Although recent data suggest that stimulants are safe and effective in the majority of patients with these two diagnoses, some patients are unable to tolerate stimulants because of effects on their tics[cite: 14]. In these patients, α2-agonists, such as guanfacine (Tenex), are indicated for their effectiveness in both reducing tics and in treating some symptoms of ADHD, particularly impulsivity, hyperactivity, and associated aggression[cite: 14].
